summaries.example: Imagine a blue cloth sample in a tailor’s shop. It has a size and shape, but its important job is to show color and texture. Goodman calls this exemplifying: the sample has a feature and points our attention to that feature. A painting can work in a similar way by showing colors, shapes, or even sadness through a metaphor.
summaries.summary: Nelson Goodman’s aesthetics explains art through symbols. A painting, song, dance, or building can refer to things and can help organize our experience. Goodman says that art and science are not complete opposites: both can help us understand the world. He also says that our classifications and habits affect what we notice. A picture is not realistic simply because it resembles its subject; it may look realistic because its way of showing things is familiar to us. Art can refer by denoting something, by exemplifying a feature, or by expressing something through metaphor. Goodman also studies how different symbol systems affect whether artworks have originals and copies, performances, or scores. His larger idea is that artworks can help make new ways of seeing and understanding the worlds we live in.
key_ideas: Goodman thinks artworks are symbols, much like words, maps, scientific ideas, and everyday signs.
Art does not only show feelings or beauty. It can help us notice, classify, and understand things.
Symbols can point to things in different ways. They can name something, show a feature, or use a metaphor.
What seems realistic or familiar in art depends partly on habits and learned ways of seeing.
Different arts use symbols differently. A painting and a musical score do not work in exactly the same way.
summaries.why_it_matters: This view encourages us to treat art as a serious way of learning, not merely as decoration or entertainment. It helps explain why a museum visit, a song, or a story can change what we notice. It also gives us tools for thinking about originals, copies, realistic pictures, artistic styles, and the different rules used by painting, music, dance, and language.

important_terms.definition: Something that stands for, points to, or helps us identify something else.
A way a symbol points to something. A name can label an object, while a sample can show a feature.
Having a feature and also pointing back to that feature, like a cloth sample showing a color.
A symbol system’s way of organizing marks and meanings, such as words, pictures, or musical signs.
The idea that art can help us understand and even build the ways we see the world.

questions_to_think_about: Can a picture teach you to notice something you had not noticed before?
What features does a favorite song or painting show or bring to your attention?
Why might two people see the same picture differently?
Is a copy of a painting the same artwork as the original?

summaries.example: Consider two performances of the same symphony. One follows every note in the score but sounds lifeless; another is exciting but changes one note. Goodman’s theory separates identity from artistic value. If the score is a genuine notation, the first technically belongs to the work, while the second may not, even though listeners may value the second more. This shows why Goodman distinguishes what makes an instance a work from what makes it a good performance.
summaries.summary: Goodman presents aesthetics as part of a broader theory of symbols, classification, knowledge, and reality. Artworks are symbols, but symbolizing is not one uniform activity. Denotation labels or classifies; exemplification displays selected features while referring to the labels for them; expression is metaphorical exemplification. These functions depend on symbol systems, whose syntactic and semantic rules determine how symbols operate. Goodman’s account of depiction rejects the idea that resemblance alone explains representation. Pictures belong to dense, relatively replete systems in which many visible differences can be significant, and realism is connected to familiar conventions of representation. His theory of notation also explains why authenticity matters differently across the arts. Paintings are autographic because their production histories distinguish originals from forgeries, whereas music and some other arts are allographic because works can have multiple compliant performances or inscriptions. Goodman separates ontological identity from artistic merit: a performance can qualify as an instance of a work without being excellent. Finally, he argues that art and science both advance understanding. Through denotation, metaphor, exemplification, and expression, artworks help construct and revise the versions of reality through which we perceive the world.
key_ideas: Goodman treats aesthetics as closely connected to epistemology: artworks contribute to understanding by classifying and reorganizing experience.
A symbol’s function depends on the symbol system in which it operates. The same object may denote, exemplify, or metaphorically refer in different contexts.
Pictures are not explained simply by resemblance. Pictorial systems are dense, so even small differences in marks may matter; realism is largely tied to familiarity and convention.
Exemplification is selective. A tailor’s swatch exemplifies color and texture, not every feature it possesses. Goodman uses this idea to explain artistic expression.
Notation helps determine the identity of works. Painting is generally autographic, while music and literature can be allographic in different ways; architecture is a mixed case.
Goodman’s constructivism allows multiple correct versions of the world. Art, science, language, and ordinary perception can all contribute to worldmaking, though versions may still be right or wrong.
summaries.why_it_matters: Goodman’s approach connects questions usually treated separately: what pictures represent, how artworks express, why originals matter, what makes a performance an instance of a work, and how art relates to knowledge. It also challenges the assumption that art is primarily opposed to science or that aesthetic experience is detached from cognition. At the same time, the entry notes unresolved issues in the framework, including how pictorial reference is established, how systems explain an artwork’s selecting some features rather than others, and whether the proposed rules fully capture artistic practice.

important_terms.definition: The basic relation of standing for or pointing to something; Goodman analyzes it as occurring through several different modes.
A symbol’s relation to what it labels, such as a name to a person or a predicate to the things it classifies.
Reference that combines possession of a feature with directing attention back to the label for that feature.
Metaphorical exemplification: an artwork appears to possess and display a feature it cannot literally possess, such as sadness.
A connected set of symbols with syntactic rules for combining them and semantic rules governing their reference.
A system in which symbols and what they refer to are sufficiently distinct and determinable; standard musical notation is a main example.
An art in which the original-versus-forgery distinction matters, as in painting; the work depends on its production history.
An art in which instances can be produced through compliance with a score or other notation, as in music.

questions_to_think_about: Does resemblance explain why a picture represents its subject, or does a learned symbol system do more of the work?
Can an artwork express sadness or movement without literally possessing those properties?
Should a performance with one wrong note count as an instance of the same musical work?
How can historical knowledge—such as knowing that a painting is an original—change what we perceive?
If there is no single essence of art, what makes a symbolic activity artistic in a particular situation?

summaries.example: Suppose your class uses a map of the school. A thick line may mark a wall, a blue shape may mark a pond, and a star may mark the office. The map does not resemble every part of the school in all ways. You understand it because you know the symbol system. If a new map uses unfamiliar colors or shapes, it may seem confusing at first. After learning its rules, you may find it clear. Goodman says artworks often work this way: our habits and learned systems affect what we see as meaningful or realistic.
summaries.summary: Nelson Goodman’s aesthetics is part of a larger theory about how symbols help people understand and organize reality. He treats paintings, music, dance, language, diagrams, and scientific theories as symbol-based activities rather than placing art in a completely separate realm. The central relation is reference, or standing for something, but reference has different forms. Denotation labels or classifies; exemplification presents a feature while referring to the label for that feature; and expression occurs when a work metaphorically exemplifies a feature, such as sadness or energy. Goodman insists that these functions depend on symbol systems and their rules. This also explains why pictures are not simply copies of what they show. Resemblance can be found in many ways, so convention and familiarity help determine which similarities matter. Goodman’s account of notation distinguishes arts according to how their works are identified. Paintings are generally autographic because their production history matters, while music and some other arts are allographic because performances can count through compliance with a score. The larger conclusion is that art contributes to knowledge by changing classifications, perception, and understanding. Like science, it can participate in constructing ways of inhabiting a world, although Goodman does not say that every version is equally successful or correct.
key_ideas: Goodman argues that art, science, and ordinary thinking all use symbols to classify and understand experience.
Whether a symbol is literal, metaphorical, denoting, or exemplifying depends on the system and context in which it is used.
He rejects the simple idea that pictures represent things only because they look like them. Familiar conventions help determine what counts as realistic.
Notation matters for artwork identity. A score can define which performances count as performances of a musical work, while a painting usually remains tied to its original object.
Goodman distinguishes identity from value. Something can technically be an instance of a work without being a good or interesting instance.
His idea of worldmaking says that different symbol systems can produce different, sometimes competing, ways of organizing reality without making every version equally correct.
summaries.why_it_matters: Goodman gives students a way to think about art beyond the question “Is it beautiful?” His theory asks what an artwork refers to, what it shows, which rules make it meaningful, and how it changes our habits of seeing. These ideas are useful when comparing a painting with a map, a song with a score, or an original with a copy. They also show why disagreements about art can involve different symbol systems and standards, not just different personal tastes.

important_terms.definition: A mark, object, sound, or picture that stands for or helps us understand something else.
The relationship between a symbol and what it stands for; Goodman describes several kinds of reference.
When a label points to the things it names or classifies, such as the word “blue” applying to blue objects.
When something both has a feature and points attention to that feature, like a fabric sample showing color or texture.
When an artwork appears to show a feature through a nonliteral transfer, such as a painting expressing sadness.
A group of symbols plus rules for how they are formed and how they connect to what they mean.
A carefully organized symbol system in which marks and meanings can be distinguished and matched in determinate ways.
An artwork type where an original and a forgery are importantly different because the work’s history of production matters.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a map need a key, and could a painting need one too?
What is the difference between an object possessing a feature and exemplifying it?
Can a picture of a fictional creature represent something even if no such creature exists?
Why might authenticity matter for a painting but not for a musical performance made from a copied score?
How can two descriptions of the same world make different changes seem important?
